paragraphs: Workvivo was the **employee experience platform**, with messaging adapted by persona. The challenge was standing out in a crowded AI-native employee experience market.

overview.eyebrow: Making product messaging a source of truth—not another document to copy
overview.lead: AI can generate content quickly. Keeping that content accurate, approved and consistent across teams is the harder problem.
overview.learning: If every AI tool gets its own version of your positioning, you have automated message drift.

caseStudy.eyebrow: Making approved messaging reusable across teams and AI tools
contribution: Owned the project and defined the content model, approval workflow and acceptance criteria
Directed AI-assisted implementation of the validation and change-proposal foundation
Tested exact edits and failure scenarios, then simplified the authoring approach

sections.title: The problem
paragraphs: Product messaging is reused across sales decks, launch materials, websites and AI prompts. Marketing, Sales and PMM need to adapt the story for different products, personas and assets while keeping claims accurate and the narrative consistent. Each adaptation creates another opportunity for wording to lose its context, evidence or approval status.

AI makes that content easier to produce and distribute. It also makes it more important to know which messages are current, supported and approved. I designed a structured messaging system to make reuse more reliable while preserving PMM ownership.

sections.title: My role and approach
paragraphs: I defined the content model, approval workflow and acceptance criteria, then directed AI-assisted implementation and tested how the system handled changes and failures. The model separates product facts from positioning, connects messages to their supporting sources, and gives content explicit ownership and review states.

The authoring pilot changed my approach. When the custom interface made it difficult to find and review the actual wording, I paused its expansion and prioritised familiar document editing, history and comments. Governance depends on people being able to understand and approve their own changes.

sections.title: How the system works
paragraphs: The intended change cycle is straightforward: a PMM edits wording, the system identifies the exact changes and checks them, and a human reviews the proposal before it becomes canonical. The implemented foundation prepares validated candidate changes and a receipt for review.
items: Edit: start from a known version of the message and submit the exact intended wording
Check: compare the edit with its baseline, preserve untouched fields and validate the candidate content
Review: retain the proposed change and its receipt for a human decision
Recover: stop when the underlying message has changed, so the author can compare versions and reconcile the edit
details: Typed objects separate product truth, buyer context, proof, messaging, design and asset recipes
Git records versions; Python and JSON Schema validate structure and references offline
An identity binding connects each authoring field to its canonical object; a deterministic compiler produces candidate files and a change receipt

sections.title: The decisions that mattered
items: Separate facts from positioning: product authority establishes what can be claimed; messaging determines how to communicate it for a buyer
Preserve exact edits: compile the wording the PMM submitted and leave other fields intact
Keep approval human: a successful technical check does not approve a claim or authorize publication
Make conflicts recoverable: preserve the original, submitted and current versions so the author can resolve a stale edit
Simplify authoring: prove one reliable change cycle in a familiar document workflow before adding more custom automation

sections.title: What I built and tested
paragraphs: The project produced a working foundation for validating structured messaging and proposing controlled changes for review. Development checks cover exact wording, untouched-field preservation, placeholders, stale edits, changed bindings and recovery from partial failures.

To make that behavior inspectable, I ran the existing compiler against a temporary local fixture using invented wording. One text edit produced a validated candidate and a change receipt. A separate comparison against a newer message returned STALE_AUTHORING_VIEW with no proposed changes.

sections.title: What I learned
paragraphs: The central design question was how to make messaging easier to reuse while keeping people accountable for its meaning and approval. The pilot showed that the collaboration experience is part of that governance: a technically controlled workflow still fails if the author cannot easily find and review the wording.
I would now prove the simplest complete human change cycle first, then add automation where it removes effort without obscuring ownership.

caseStudy.context: HQ Agent extended Workvivo beyond communications and employee experience into trusted enterprise answers, search, self-service, and agentic task execution. It sat at the intersection of enterprise knowledge, RAG, permissions, employee experience, and Zoom’s broader AI technology.

overview.eyebrow: Turning curiosity into a story people can explore
overview.lead: A national result tells you who won. I wanted to understand what sat beneath it: the differences between places, the change between rounds, and the experience of Brazilians voting abroad. I turned those questions into Brazil in Red, a bilingual interactive atlas.
overview.learning: A chart can be accurate and still tell the wrong story. Choosing what to compare is part of the strategy.

story.title: Finding the story beneath the result
paragraphs: The starting point was personal curiosity. As I explored the results, the question grew: how could I bring the national picture, regional differences, and overseas vote into one experience that made sense to someone arriving without all that context?

I chose to give the atlas an editorial direction, then let readers investigate it. The page moves from the national result to changes between rounds, Brazilian states, and voters abroad. That sequence gives people a way into the subject before asking them to navigate a map or interpret a table.
story.label: Editorial direction

story.title: A guided story, with room to explore
paragraphs: I set the questions, directed the research and AI-assisted build, and shaped the structure, visual direction, and interaction design. The published experience covers 27 Brazilian federal units and 31 selected overseas countries and territories, with English and Portuguese views.

I wanted the narrative and the interactive elements to work together. A reader can follow the page for the main patterns, then use the maps, round selectors, regional filters, and comparison tables to examine a place that matters to them. Headings, labels, and visual hierarchy had to support both ways of reading.
story.label: Experience design

visual.title: Inside the atlas
visual.alt: The atlas opening screen with its national result comparison.
visual.caption: Start with the national picture, then explore places and comparisons.

story.title: The choices behind the comparisons
paragraphs: The most useful iterations came from questioning what a reader could reasonably conclude from each visual. I pushed for changes wherever an apparently simple comparison could imply something the data did not establish:
items: Give each percentage a clear meaning. A candidate’s share, the winner’s share, and a change between rounds answer different questions. The labels needed to identify the candidate, round, and voting basis.

Make the rounds comparable. Round one includes other candidates. The atlas distinguishes all-valid-vote shares from a comparison recalculated around the two finalists, and separates a change in winner from the size of the swing.

Choose the right level of context. Highlighting Ireland and France did not tell the whole European story. I asked for a regional view alongside the individual examples, so the selection of places would not carry more weight than it should.

Keep interpretation within the evidence. Aggregate changes show how results differed between rounds; they do not establish how individual people switched their votes. Source links and methodology notes give readers a way to examine those boundaries.
story.label: Strategic judgment

story.title: Making space for the people behind the numbers
paragraphs: I also wanted the atlas to convey what participation involved. I asked to include stories of people travelling by boat, offering lifts, and helping others reach the polls alongside the political context and disputes. That widened the story from the outcome of voting to the effort people made to take part.

The resulting project brings research, editorial judgment, and product design into one public experience. It reflects an approach I bring to product marketing: find the question people care about, turn complexity into a clear story, and make it easy to go deeper.
story.label: Human context

caseStudy.eyebrow: Building an AI-enabled PMM operating model
caseStudy.context: AI-first Product Marketing is not simply a team using ChatGPT. Shauna has been exploring how AI can change the operating model of PMM itself—and where human judgment must remain accountable.
caseStudy.challenge: High-value PMM time disappears into retrieval, repeated seller questions, monitoring, synthesis, recurring research, and first-pass analysis. The strategic question is which work requires human judgment and which work can be processed or automated.
caseStudy.insight: AI does more of the processing. PMM remains accountable for the thinking. Retrieval, extraction, monitoring, classification, and repeatable analysis can accelerate; positioning, pricing, claims, category strategy, and executive recommendations still need accountable judgment.

caseStudy.outcome: The result is a growing set of practical systems that increase PMM leverage while keeping strategic accountability human. The tools are not the proof; the workflow design and operating choices are.
caseStudy.learning: Technical expertise for a PMM is the ability to understand enough of the system to make better product, pricing, trust, and go-to-market decisions.

caseStudy.eyebrow: Turning a résumé into an evidence-grounded conversation
caseStudy.context: A static portfolio can show the work, but it cannot adapt to the question a recruiter, hiring manager, or technical stakeholder actually wants answered. Shauna designed a live ElevenLabs experience that lets visitors explore her career, case studies, technical builds, and working principles through voice or text. She also created a voice persona from her own voice and gave the agent a defined personality so the experience feels recognisably hers without pretending to be her.
caseStudy.challenge: The agent needed to be persuasive without becoming a hype machine. It had to answer broad career questions quickly, go deep on named projects, distinguish work Shauna built from products she marketed, link back to public evidence, and avoid turning company outcomes or technical fluency into unsupported personal claims.
caseStudy.insight: A credible portfolio agent is a voice, context, workflow, and evaluation problem—not simply a prompt. Better answers came from defining the persona, separating durable rules from retrievable evidence, routing different intents to specialist answer modes, comparing model outputs, and analysing failures where attribution, role fit, or technical ownership could drift.
contribution: Created a custom voice persona from her own recorded voice and defined its personality, tone, conversational style, and answer behaviour
Engineered the system prompts, answer contract, evidence standard, and guardrails
Designed a modular knowledge base around career, technical builds, case studies, learning, recognition, and a canonical claim ledger
Built the workflow and intent-routing conditions for technical questions, case-study deep dives, career history, working style, and role-fit pressure tests
Compared outputs from multiple models and analysed response quality, grounding, tone, and failure patterns
Ran iterative manual and structured tests, then refined prompts, routes, knowledge, and response behaviour
Documented procedures for how the agent handles common intents, evidence, uncertainty, testing, updates, and release review
Integrated the ElevenLabs conversational widget into a responsive GitHub Pages portfolio
Built a Node-based source pipeline that converts maintained Markdown into upload-ready HTML knowledge documents
decisions: Use voice and text as the interface, while keeping public case-study links as the evidence layer
Keep compact identity and claim rules in always-on prompt context; retrieve longer case-study material only when relevant
Route by visitor intent rather than forcing one general prompt to handle every conversation style
Answer technical questions decisively with concrete build evidence, then add ownership boundaries only where they prevent a false inference
Keep knowledge sources versioned privately, with a public system overview and integration code for visitors to inspect
Treat live platform configuration and repository evidence as separate states; published files document the design but do not prove every console setting is active
architecture: ElevenLabs Conversational AI provides the live voice and text runtime embedded through its web component
A custom voice persona created from Shauna's own voice provides a consistent spoken identity, supported by defined personality and conversation rules
A main-agent workflow coordinates specialist intent routes for career, technical evidence, case-study depth, working style, and fit assessment
Two compact prompt documents hold identity, personality, answer policy, and claim controls in persistent context
Nine focused knowledge documents are configured for RAG so the agent retrieves only the evidence relevant to the question
A canonical claim ledger separates externally verified facts, public artifacts, self-reported experience, company context, and work still in progress
Absolute portfolio and repository links let answers point visitors back to inspectable evidence
tooling: ElevenLabs Conversational AI for the agent runtime, custom voice persona, speech interface, workflow, model configuration, and knowledge retrieval
Prompt engineering and conversation design for personality, response structure, routing, and behavioural boundaries
Structured evaluation and qualitative analysis for comparing model outputs and finding recurring failure patterns
HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript for the portfolio and widget integration
Markdown and structured front matter as the editable knowledge source
Node.js for deterministic Markdown-to-HTML knowledge builds
Git and GitHub for versioning, public evidence, and GitHub Pages deployment
Codex and other AI development tools for implementation support, with Shauna retaining the product, content, and claim decisions
safeguards: Third-person identity prevents the agent from impersonating Shauna
Attribution rules distinguish products marketed, systems built, tools used, and concepts studied
Hard claim rules block invented metrics, sole credit for company outcomes, and unsupported production-engineering claims
Specialist routing reduces context collisions between technical proof, career history, project narratives, and role-fit assessment
Public links and evidence labels make provenance visible instead of asking visitors to trust generated prose
A bounded answer pattern keeps voice responses concise and avoids turning narrow questions into résumé recitations
validation: Fifteen acceptance questions cover the most common recruiter and technical-review journeys
A 13-question evaluation set tests positioning, technical evidence, ownership boundaries, unsupported claims, role-fit nuance, leadership, and concise voice responses
Multiple model outputs were tested against comparable prompts to evaluate answer quality and trade-offs
Repeated live voice and text tests exposed issues in tone, grounding, routing, concision, and claim boundaries
Test analysis informed successive changes to prompts, model choices, workflow routes, knowledge sources, and guardrails
Explicit pass criteria and documented procedures make review repeatable rather than purely subjective
Knowledge documents carry version and review dates so content drift can be traced
Repository checks can validate source completeness and regenerated HTML before the knowledge pack is uploaded
Live conversational quality still requires manual testing in ElevenLabs after knowledge or workflow configuration changes
caseStudy.outcome: The result is a live, inspectable portfolio interface that demonstrates more than familiarity with AI tools. It shows Shauna's ability to shape a voice persona, engineer prompts, build an intent-routing workflow, configure retrieval and guardrails, compare model behaviour, analyse tests, and translate the technical decisions into a clear professional story. The agent runs on ElevenLabs; Shauna designed, configured, tested, documented, and integrated the experience rather than engineering the underlying voice models or platform runtime.
caseStudy.learning: The quality of an agent is shaped less by the cleverness of one prompt than by the discipline of its context, routing, evidence, evaluation, and boundaries.

overview.eyebrow: Turning analyst relations into a strategic market leadership programme
overview.lead: When Workvivo's dedicated analyst relations owner left, I took on the remit alongside leading Product Marketing. I built a repeatable programme that strengthened our existing position and helped open up adjacent markets.
overview.learning: If analyst relations only starts when a report is due, someone else’s calendar is setting your strategic agenda.

caseStudy.context: Workvivo evolved from an underdog employee app into a recognised Employee Experience Platform and later a broader AI-native employee-experience story. Analyst understanding had to evolve with the product and company narrative.
caseStudy.challenge: Market leadership is not created by a single briefing. It requires a consistent point of view, credible evidence, strong customer proof, disciplined claims, and alignment across products that are evolving at different speeds.
caseStudy.insight: Analyst relations works best as a connected category system—not a calendar of submissions. The analyst narrative, evidence base, competitive position, customer proof, and GTM story need to reinforce one another.

decisions: Build a durable category story rather than chase individual rankings

caseStudy.outcome: Workvivo received recognition across Gartner, Forrester, G2, ClearBox, Gartner Peer Insights, and SoftwareReviews. Shauna played a substantial role in the program; independent analysts and reviewers controlled their own outcomes.
caseStudy.learning: Influence without control demands evidence, consistency, and patience. Strong analyst relations makes the company easier to understand before it tries to make it look impressive.

overview.eyebrow: Turning a market disruption into a clear reason to choose Workvivo
overview.lead: When Meta announced Workplace's closure, its customers had to move. But Workvivo still had to earn their choice.
overview.learning: A competitor’s exit creates urgency. It does not create a reason to choose you.

caseStudy.context: Meta announced the closure of Workplace. Workvivo was named Meta’s only preferred migration partner, creating a major, time-bound market opportunity and a highly visible competitive GTM motion.
caseStudy.challenge: Workvivo had to move quickly while differentiating against competitors, reducing migration risk, addressing customer uncertainty, enabling sellers, and converting a temporary market event into durable commercial opportunity.
caseStudy.insight: The winning story needed to combine urgency with reassurance. Migration could not feel like a technical transfer alone; it needed to feel like a credible path from a closing platform to a stronger long-term employee experience.
